content: The authors acknowledge that the use of willingness-to-pay (WTP) thresholds, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), is a topic of significant debate. However, interventions can be considered cost-effective if evaluated using the World Health Organization (WHO) WTP threshold of three times a country’s GDP per capita. For example, in The Gambia, this threshold is $1,460. This study is the only cost-effectiveness analysis of screening and treatment in LMIC settings that the authors have identified. HIV testing for couples and partners has been implemented in various settings, including antenatal care (ANC), community-based tuberculosis (TB) services, antiretroviral therapy (ART) services, and premarital health visits. Testing the partners of women attending ANC is a particular focus in the 21 priority countries for the elimination of mother-to-child transmission (eMTCT) of HIV. These countries, which are highly endemic for hepatitis B virus (HBV), present a unique opportunity to integrate concurrent HBV testing for partners of women with chronic HBV (CHB) or chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, especially if risk factors are present. In high HBV-prevalence settings, adolescents aged 10–19 years fall into two groups requiring HBV testing: (1) those undiagnosed but exposed perinatally or in early childhood, and (2) those who acquire HBV sexually (e.g., through early sexual activity, multiple partners, or contact with a person with CHB) or via injecting drug use. Perinatally infected adolescents urgently need diagnosis to link them to HBV monitoring and care, initiating antiviral treatment when clinically indicated. Many highly endemic HBV settings have a significant number of undiagnosed perinatally infected adolescents. Those without evidence of CHB should be vaccinated if they have not already received the vaccine. Adolescents and young adults in many countries may have missed HBV vaccination due to the timing of universal infant vaccination programs. Universal HBV immunization, including a birth dose within 24 hours of birth, is critical to preventing mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HBV. However, many countries face economic and logistical barriers to implementing this intervention. Infants born to mothers diagnosed with HBV or HCV should be followed up and routinely offered early infant diagnosis (EID). This can be achieved through routine provider-initiated testing and counseling (PITC) in health facilities, particularly in high-prevalence settings, and by testing family members of index cases when appropriate. HBV testing services for infants should aim to identify HBV-infected infants as early as possible. While a conservative approach to treatment is often indicated, children born to HBV-infected mothers should be screened early to organize monitoring for liver disease progression and to facilitate testing and vaccination of household contacts. In high-prevalence settings, HBV and HCV testing for mothers and infants should be routinely available through various services, including child health services, immunization clinics, under-5 clinics, malnutrition services, well-child services, TB clinics, and services for hospitalized or sick children, as well as for orphans and vulnerable children. Testing family members of index cases is essential, as gaps in HBV testing and documentation of children’s HBV status in HBV-positive families represent significant missed opportunities. These gaps can be addressed by following up with families identified in ANC or facilities offering HBV testing. In all settings, children with an HBV-positive parent or close household contact should be prioritized for HBV testing. For hepatitis C virus (HCV), targeted risk-based screening is recommended for high-risk populations, including people who inject drugs (PWID), men who have sex with men (MSM), immigrants, recipients of blood transfusions or blood products, sex workers, and healthcare workers. General population screening or screening of selected subpopulations (e.g., pregnant women, those with elevated alanine aminotransferase [ALT] levels, infants, schoolchildren, and adolescents) may also be considered. Birth cohort screening, based on specific age cutoffs, and repeat screening every five years are additional strategies. Testing strategies should be evaluated for their impact, cost, and cost-effectiveness in different populations and settings. HCV is a global public health burden and a leading cause of liver failure and hepatocellular carcinoma. Transmission occurs predominantly in high-risk populations, such as PWID, people in prisons, mobile populations, indigenous populations, MSM, and sex workers. PWID are particularly at high risk of HCV infection, with prevalence rates exceeding 60–80% in many countries. MSM, especially those living with HIV, are also at increased risk of acquiring HCV sexually. The advent of highly effective, short-duration therapies has prioritized HCV testing, linking infected individuals to care, and curing HCV before the onset of cirrhosis or end-stage liver disease. However, low rates of diagnosis and linkage to care remain significant challenges, with fewer than 15% of the estimated 180 million chronically infected individuals aware of their diagnosis. Hepatitis B and C testing and diagnosis are critical for entry into prevention and treatment cascades. Testing identifies those who are positive, links them to care, and provides counseling to reduce transmission. Three key approaches to HCV screening include targeted risk-based screening, birth cohort screening, and general population screening. Targeted screening focuses on high-risk groups, such as PWID, people in prisons, MSM, and healthcare workers. Birth cohort screening identifies individuals exposed to HCV through historical sources, such as unscreened blood supplies. In summary, comprehensive testing strategies for HBV and HCV should prioritize high-risk populations, integrate testing into existing healthcare services, and address gaps in diagnosis and care. These efforts are essential to reducing the burden of viral hepatitis and improving health outcomes globally.
